nodes.title: The Company
nodes.summary: Bajaj Finance Limited (BFL), a leading diversified NBFC, operates across 10 categories including consumer lending, SME, auto, rural, gold loans, and deposits. Classified as an upper-layer NBFC since September 2022, it has 4,263 locations. FY2025 consolidated results show 26% AUM growth to ₹416,661 crore, 16% PAT growth to ₹16,779 crore, RoA of 4.57%, ROE of 19.19%, and CRAR of 21.93%. BHFL completed a ₹6,560 crore IPO, reducing BFL's stake to 88.75%. Promoter warrants converted to equity. Customer franchise grew 22% to 101.82 million, new loans 43.42 million, and the Bajaj Finserv App had 70.57 million customers. NII, NTI, and operating profit rose, while impairment increased 72%.

nodes.title: Foreign currency risk

Foreign currency risk
BFL is exposed to foreign currency fluctuation risk mainly for its External Commercial Borrowings (ECB). BFL’s borrowings in foreign currency are governed by RBI guidelines (RBI master direction RBI/FED/2018-19/67 dated 26 March 2019 and updated from time to time) which requires entities raising ECB for a maturity less than five years to hedge minimum 70% of its ECB principal and coupon. Bajaj Finance considers foreign currency exchange rates, tenure of ECB and its fully hedged costs while raising funds through ECB. nodes.title: Bajaj Housing Finance Limited (BHFL)
nodes.summary: Bajaj Housing Finance Limited (BHFL), a subsidiary of Bajaj Finance, is a non-deposit taking housing finance company registered with NHB since 2015 and categorized as Upper Layer NBFC. It started lending in July 2017, reached AUM of ₹114,684 crore as of March 2025, and listed on NSE and BSE via a ₹6,560 crore IPO in September 2024, diluting BFL's stake to 88.75%. BHFL offers a full mortgage suite: home loans, loans against property, lease rental discounting, developer financing, and partnership/services, catering to salaried, self-employed, and professional customers across prime, near prime, and affordable segments, plus commercial products for developers, HNIs, REITs, sovereign wealth funds, and corporates. It holds AAA/stable and A1+ credit ratings. FY2025 performance highlights include AUM up 26%, NII up 20%, NTI up 23%, impairment up 31%, PBT up 28%, PAT up 25%, and capital adequacy ratio of 28.24%. Tables detail AUM by product and standalone financials (total income, interest/finance charges, net total income, operating expenses, pre-impairment operating profit, impairment, PBT, PAT, other comprehensive income, total comprehensive income, EPS). Bajaj Financial Securities Limited (Bajaj Broking), a wholly-owned subsidiary registered with SEBI as stockbroker and depository participant, expanded to 46 locations and 48 branches, serving over 9.7 lakh clients. FY2025 highlights: customer franchise up 40% to over 979,000, MTF book up 18% to ₹4,505 crore, NII up 122% to ₹249 crore, NTI up 58% to ₹441 crore, PBT up 158% to ₹183 crore, PAT up 148% to ₹139 crore. It serves over 66,000 HNI clients with dedicated call-in-trade, customized brokerage plans, trading terminals, and expansion in Tier 2 and 3 cities.

It reports FY2025 onboarding of 2.6 lakh new users, total client base of 9.2 lakh, 2.7 million app downloads, and 4.2 app rating. The proprietary trading division aims for superior risk-adjusted returns, generated 15% return vs Nifty 50's 3% in FY2025 with better risk metrics, half the volatility, allocated fund of ₹250 crore, and plans to scale up while building quantitative and statistical arbitrage capabilities using machine learning and quantitative analysis. Margin Trading Facility (MTF) for HNIs and retail allows up to 4X margin on over 1,000 securities; MTF AUM grew 18% to ₹4,505 crore as of March 31, 2025, from ₹3,817 crore. Online presence was enhanced via website and app upgrades in product features, tools, and service. nodes.title: Objective
nodes.summary:
Objective
T he Company’s objective is to maintain appropriate levels of capital to support its business strategy taking into account the regulatory, economic and commercial environment. The Company aims to maintain a strong capital base to support the risks inherent to its business and growth strategies. The Company endeavours to maintain a higher capital base than the mandated regulatory capital at all times.

nodes.title: Planning

It details dividend distributions, post-reporting events, and fair value measurement with a three-level hierarchy and valuation methodologies. Financial risk management is comprehensively addressed: liquidity risk (ALCO monitoring, borrowing mix, liquidity buffer, contingency funding), market risk (interest rate, price, and foreign currency risk with sensitivity analyses and hedging), and credit risk (three-stage classification, ECL approach, collateral, guarantees, concentration risk, and sensitivity analysis).

nodes.title: (ii) Regulatory capital

It covers funding support to subsidiaries, associates, and investee companies. It presents regulatory capital details (Tier I, Tier II, total capital, risk-weighted assets, and CRAR for 2024 and 2025), dividend distributions made and proposed (final and special interim dividends with percentages), events after the reporting date, and fair value measurement including the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1 and 2).

nodes.title: 48 Fair values
nodes.summary: The text defines fair value as an exit price and outlines a three-level fair value hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs). It describes the Company's valuation framework, including internal assessment, benchmarking, model validation, and governance. Valuation methodologies for various financial instruments are detailed: FVTPL investments (Level 1), unquoted FVOCI equity (Level 3 discounted cash flow), quoted FVOCI equity (Level 1), and derivatives like CCIRS and forwards (Level 2). It notes that amortized cost instruments' carrying values approximate fair value for short-term items. Quantitative disclosures for recurring fair value measurements as at 31 March 2025 and 2024 are presented, showing assets and liabilities by hierarchy level. Level 3 reconciliation shows changes in unobservable inputs, and sensitivity analysis for Level 3 equity instruments is provided. Fair values of financial instruments measured at amortised cost are disclosed with carrying values and fair value hierarchy levels for both years. The Company has no non-recurring fair value measurements.

nodes.title: 49 Financial risk management
nodes.summary: This text covers financial risk management, detailing major risks from financial instruments: liquidity, market, and credit risk. For each risk, it describes the nature and sources (e.g., liquidity risk from cash flow mismatches, market risk from interest rate/foreign exchange/equity fluctuations, credit risk from counterparty default), the executive governance structure (Board's Risk Management Committee, Asset Liability Committee, Chief Risk Officer), and the measurement, monitoring, and management approaches. Measurement includes gap analysis, liquidity coverage ratio, Value at Risk, PV01, and default metrics. Monitoring involves ALCO reviews, stress tests, and portfolio assessments. Management includes treasury actions, high-quality liquid assets, liquidity buffers, contingency funding plans, and robust control frameworks.

nodes.title: (a) Liquidity risk
nodes.summary: The text covers liquidity risk management, detailing ALCO monitoring of asset-liability mismatches, a diversified borrowing mix including bank borrowings, money markets, ECBs, deposits, and securitisation. nodes.title: (iii) Foreign currency risk

nodes.title: Financial Assets: Derecognition and Impairment Accounting Policies
key_items: Impairment of financial assets - General approach
nodes.summary: The page details accounting policies for derecognition and impairment of financial assets. Derecognition occurs when cash flow rights expire, or assets are transferred with substantially all risks and rewards, including partial assignments, servicing rights, and write-offs, with gains/losses recognized in profit or loss. Write-offs occur when recovery is not reasonably expected. The general impairment approach recognizes expected credit losses (ECL) for all financial assets except FVTPL and equity instruments. A staging methodology applies: Stage 1 (12-month ECL) for no significant credit risk increase; Stage 2 (lifetime ECL) for significant increase; Stage 3 (lifetime ECL) for default or objective impairment evidence. Financial assets are written off when no realistic recovery prospect exists, with possible enforcement activities.

nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: derecognition of financial liabilities; income taxes including current and deferred tax recognition, measurement, and offsetting; property, plant and equipment measured at cost less depreciation/impairment with straight-line depreciation and derecognition gains/losses; intangible assets including internally generated, amortized over five years, and derecognition treatment; provisions and contingent liabilities recognition and disclosure; leases as lessee (lease liability and right-of-use asset measurement, short-term lease exemption, modification) and as lessor (finance leases, net investment accounting); and fair value measurement using valuation techniques and fair value hierarchy levels.

nodes.title: Lease Accounting Policies: Liability and Right-of-Use Assets
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting policies under Ind AS 116 for leases, specifically office premises and servers. It covers initial and subsequent measurement of lease liability, including discounting using incremental borrowing cost, interest accrual, payments, and remeasurement for reassessments or modifications. It also details initial and subsequent measurement of right-of-use assets using the cost model, including depreciation on a straight-line basis and impairment adjustments, with remeasurement aligned to lease liability changes. Additionally, it notes the exemption for short-term leases (12 months or less), where lease payments are expensed over the lease term without recognizing assets or liabilities.

nodes.title: Modification of lease
nodes.summary: The text covers lease modification accounting for lessees and lessors, including remeasurement of lease liability and finance lease receivables. It details fair value measurement, including valuation techniques and hierarchy levels. It also covers derivative financial instruments, including forwards, swaps, and cross-currency swaps, their initial and subsequent measurement, and hedge accounting. Hedge accounting includes designation, documentation, effectiveness assessment, and specific treatment for cash flow hedges, including OCI recognition, reclassification, and discontinuation.

nodes.title: Derivative Financial Instruments and Hedge Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page outlines the Group's accounting policies for derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting. It covers the initial and subsequent measurement of derivatives at fair value, recognition of gains/losses, and classification as financial assets or liabilities. It details hedge accounting criteria, documentation requirements, and effectiveness assessment. Specifically, it explains cash flow hedges, including recognition of effective and ineffective portions, reclassification from OCI to profit or loss, and treatment upon hedge termination or forecasted transaction changes. The page also mentions fair value disclosures and classes of assets and liabilities based on nature, characteristics, risks, and fair value hierarchy.

nodes.title: Fair value hedge
nodes.summary: The text outlines the accounting policy for fair value hedges, which hedge exposure to fair value changes in recognized liabilities attributable to specific risks affecting profit or loss. It details recognition of cumulative fair value changes for hedging derivatives and hedged items in the Statement of Profit and Loss (finance costs) and Balance Sheet, classification criteria for fair value hedge relationships (e.g., fixed-rate debt for interest rate risk), and discontinuation rules when hedges expire or fail effectiveness criteria. It also covers amortization of accumulated fair value hedge adjustments for hedged items at amortized cost using the recalculated effective interest rate method upon termination, and immediate recognition in profit or loss if the hedged item is derecognized.

nodes.title: Arising from
nodes.summary: The text details financial risk management, covering liquidity, funding, market, and credit risks. It describes liquidity risk arising from cash flow timing mismatches, governed by the RMC and ALCO, and funding risk from inability to raise borrowings, long-term asset funding issues, and volatile market conditions. Measurement includes liquidity gaps and LCR; monitoring involves gap assessment, fund source calibration, and ALCO stress tests; management uses HQLA, buffers, long-term funds, and a Contingency Funding Plan. Market risk stems from interest rate, forex, and equity fluctuations, governed by RMC and ALCO. Credit risk is loss from counterparty default, governed by RMC and CRO.

nodes.title: Measurement, monitoring and management of risk
nodes.summary: The text covers financial risk management, focusing on market, credit, and liquidity risks. Market risk includes equity, exchange rate, and interest rate exposures, measured using VaR, PV01, and modified duration, monitored via key parameters and MVE analysis, and managed by the treasury team under ALCO. Credit risk is measured by default rates and other metrics, monitored by RMC and CRO, and managed through a robust control framework. Liquidity risk is monitored by ALCO to avoid mismatches, with diversified borrowings and a liquidity buffer of 5-8% of net borrowings. It details regulatory LCR compliance, a Contingency Funding Plan, and provides maturity profiles of financial liabilities and assets as of March 31, 2025, and 2024.

structure.title: Market Risk: Interest Rate Sensitivity Analysis for 2025 and 2024
structure.summary: The page covers market risk, defining it as the risk of fair value fluctuations in financial instruments due to changes in market variables like interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity prices, and credit spreads. It focuses on interest rate risk, explaining that sensitivity analysis for floating rate assets and liabilities assumes the outstanding amount at period end was outstanding for the whole year. Tables demonstrate sensitivity to a reasonably possible change in interest rates, showing the impact on profit before tax through floating rate financial assets and liabilities, with all other variables held constant. Sensitivity analyses are provided as at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2024, detailing principal outstanding and the impact on the Statement of Profit and Loss for a 1% interest rate increase and decrease on loans, debt securities, and borrowings (other than debt securities), in crore.

structure.title: (ii) Price risk
structure.summary: The text discusses price risk affecting the Group's quoted equity and derivative instruments, and how the Group manages this risk by monitoring sectors, investee performance, and mark-to-market gains/losses. It provides sensitivity analyses as at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2024, showing the impact on the Statement of Profit and Loss for a 10% increase/decrease in fair value of quoted equity shares, and a 1% increase/decrease for FVOCI debt instruments and FVTPL investments other than equity shares. Carrying values and fair values are presented in crore for each category.

structure.title: (iii) Foreign currency risk
structure.summary: The text addresses foreign currency risk, noting the Group's exposure mainly from external commercial borrowing (ECB). It cites RBI guidelines requiring minimum 70% hedging for ECBs with average maturity under 5 years, while the Group hedges 100% per its Board-approved policy. It describes evaluating fully hedged costs and managing risk via OTC derivatives like cross currency swaps and forwards with highly rated bank counterparties to mitigate credit risk. Finally, it presents the Group's foreign currency risk exposure in INR crore as of 31 March 2025 and 2024, showing hedged ECB amounts (USD 1,800 million and USD 725 million prior year) and derivative financial instrument notional amounts, with no unhedged exposure.

key_items: Classification of financial assets under various stages
structure.summary: The page presents part of the notes to consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, covering financial risk management. Section (c) defines credit risk as the risk of financial loss from customers or counterparties failing to meet repayment obligations, noting the Group's diversified lending model across secured and unsecured products and its assessment of credit quality. It then classifies financial assets into three stages: Stage 1 (no credit impairment or significant increase in credit risk; 12-month ECL), Stage 2 (significant increase in credit risk; lifetime ECL), and Stage 3 (objective evidence of impairment/default; lifetime ECL), with treatment and classification methodology detailed in note 3.3(i).

structure.title: Computation of impairment on financial instruments
structure.summary: The text details the Group's computation of impairment on financial instruments using the Expected Credit Loss (ECL) approach under Ind AS 109, covering components PD, LGD, and EAD with forward-looking macroeconomic adjustments. It explains periodic recalibration of the ECL model, including redevelopment and Board approval during the year. A table summarizes the approach for PD, EAD, and LGD across product lines like urban/rural sales finance, two/three-wheeler financing, personal loans, SME lending, gold loans, car loans, mortgages, loans against securities, and commercial lending, using empirical data and management judgment. Another table presents gross carrying values, ECL allowances, and coverage ratios stage-wise for secured and unsecured loan portfolios as at 31 March 2025 and 2024.

structure.title: Collateral valuation
structure.summary: The text covers the Group's collateral valuation practices. It states that loans are offered based on repayment ability rather than primary reliance on collateral, though collateral mitigates credit risk. It lists main collateral types by product group: hypothecation of financed products (consumer durables, vehicles, equipment), pledge of gold jewellery, mortgages of properties, pledge of securities, and plant/machinery/book debts. The Group periodically monitors collateral market value and loan-to-value metrics for high-risk customers. It exercises repossession rights, invokes SARFAESI Act and judicial remedies, and handles repossessed assets via auction or release. For loan against securities, shortfalls are recouped through part recall, additional securities, or sale. Repossessed assets are not recorded as non-current assets held for sale.

key_items: ECL sensitivity analysis to forward economic conditions and management overlay
structure.summary: The page covers three sections from financial risk management notes: guarantee cover taken on loans, including CGTMSE, CGMFU, and ECLGS schemes; analysis of concentration risk, focusing on portfolio granulisation and geographic diversification; and ECL sensitivity analysis to forward economic conditions and management overlay, detailing probability-weighted economic scenarios, periodic recalibration of ECL models, and qualitative overlays for emerging risks.

structure.title: Methodology
structure.summary: The methodology outlines the Group's use of three economic scenarios (central, upside, downside) with assigned probabilities (80%, 10%, 10%) to estimate unbiased forward-looking ECL adjustments. It details the selection of macroeconomic factors (GDP growth, bank credit, WPI, CPI, industrial production, unemployment, crude oil prices, policy interest rates) tested for correlation with default rates, with real GDP and unemployment chosen for the FEG model. Specific assumptions for unemployment (central: 8.4% to 7.6%; downside: peak 11.7% normalizing to 7.6%; upside: best case 3.4% by June 2026 then 7.6%) and real GDP (central: 6.5% moderating to 6.1%; downside: 3.3% in Q1FY2027 then 6.1%; upside: 10.3% in Q1FY2027 then 6.1%) are provided, based on external forecasts and management estimates.

structure.title: Method used for accounting for share based payment plan
structure.summary: The text details the Parent Company's fair value method for accounting for share-based payment plans using the Black-Scholes Model for stock options. It lists key assumptions (risk-free interest rate, expected life, volatility, dividend yield, share price, vesting period) and provides specific data for grants from 2021 to 2024, including option numbers and vesting terms. It notes adjustments for share subdivision and bonus shares. For the year ended 31 March 2025, the Group recognized an employee benefit expense of ₹377.00 crore (previous year ₹268.23 crore) for this plan, with an outstanding balance of ₹934.86 crore (previous year ₹711.50 crore).

structure.title: (B) Employee stock option plan of Bajaj Finserv Limited

Method used for accounting for share based payment plan
structure.summary: The text details Bajaj Housing Finance Limited's employee stock option plan, approved by the Board on 24 April 2024, for up to 5% of issued equity capital (39,09,78,763 shares of face value ₹10) under SEBI guidelines and Section 81(1A) of the Companies Act, 1956. Options vest over 1 to 5 years with continuous employment, except in death or permanent incapacity. Grants to tenured employees in managerial and leadership roles are specified, including grant dates (24-Apr-24 and 4-Jan-25), exercise prices (₹54.50 and ₹126.38), number of options granted (16,751,673 and 486,445), and their status (outstanding, vested, unvested, exercised, cancelled, expired) as of 31 March 2025. Weighted average fair values (₹24.54 and ₹51.43) and a table of exercise price ranges and weighted average remaining contractual life (6.58 years) are provided. The accounting method uses the fair value method with the Black–Scholes Model, including key assumptions: risk-free interest rate (7.05% and 6.63%), expected life (3.5–6.5 and 3.5–5.5 years), expected volatility (38.46% and 36.57%), dividend yield (nil), market price (₹54.50 and ₹126.08), and vesting periods (1–4 and 1–3 years on SLM basis).

structure.title: 50 Ultimate beneficiary
structure.summary: This note to the consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 addresses ultimate beneficiary disclosures. It states that the Group has not advanced, loaned, or invested funds—from any source—to any intermediaries with the understanding that those funds would be lent or invested in ultimate beneficiaries identified by or on behalf of the Group, nor provided guarantees or security on their behalf. Similarly, it confirms that the Parent Company and its subsidiaries BFinsec and BHFL have not received funds from any funding parties with the understanding that they would lend or invest in ultimate beneficiaries identified by or on behalf of those parties, nor provide guarantees or security on their behalf.
